solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: A consequence of what PR advisors do in bad taste

blocks.note: public relations people put a favourable slant, or spin, on the news
food that has gone off tastes bad

explanation.surface: Political spin doctors behaving tastelessly and the fallout that follows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In bad taste' reads as tasteless conduct, but it describes rotten food: milk that tastes bad is off.
explanation.definitionFit: A by-product or secondary result arising from something else is called this, so it is a kind of consequence.

clue.text: A couple of pints needed to take in article in English: 'Covid-19 Result'?

indicators.note: taking something in means swallowing it whole, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a quart is two pints
the indefinite article
taken as written
E is the standard abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A drinker's headline: two pints with an English article about the pandemic.
explanation.walkthrough: The article sits inside the two-pint measure, splitting it before its final T; the clue's quotation marks dress the definition as a newspaper headline.
explanation.definitionFit: Isolation imposed to stop infection spreading was a familiar outcome of catching or being exposed to the coronavirus in 2020.

clue.text: May, last of Tory powerful!

indicators.note: the final letter alone of the next word is kept

blocks.note: might is the past form of the verb may
end letter of the word

explanation.surface: An ironic cheer for Theresa May, the last Tory leader, as a powerful figure.
explanation.walkthrough: May looks like Theresa May, the former Conservative prime minister, but it is the verb: you may, you might.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe having great strength, force or influence, so they are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: Refs sort out defence

indicators.note: letters that are out of place have been knocked from their order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Referees ought to tidy up a team's leaky back line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort out' reads as one phrasal verb, but 'sort' joins the fodder and only 'out' signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A fortified stronghold is a place built for protection against attack, a concrete form of defence.

clue.text: see 22ac.
Cover up discharge

blocks.note: first meaning: to hide something away
second meaning: what a gland does when it releases a substance

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests hushing up someone's dismissal; the two senses of the word are pronounced alike but come from different roots.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both to conceal in a hidden place and, in biology, to produce and release a fluid.

clue.text: Make a connection with Putin's no.1 (clumsy oaf) getting elected

indicators.note: number one in a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: opening letter of the name
a lug is a big awkward lout
a candidate who is elected gets in

explanation.surface: Linking up with Putin's chief henchman, a clumsy oaf now voted into office.
explanation.walkthrough: IN for elected is a crossword staple: the winning party is in, the losers out.
explanation.definitionFit: Connecting an electrical device to the mains socket is the literal sense of this phrasal verb.

clue.text: Thwarting action means (a) less than half of Boris gets leg over

indicators.note: under half a word means only a short opening run of its letters survives
something put over others covers them on both sides, so it surrounds them

blocks.note: taken as written
two of the five letters, less than half
a leg of a journey or race is a stage

explanation.surface: Private Eye smut: Boris Johnson getting his leg over, undermining something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets his leg over' is British slang for having sex; here the word for a leg of a journey goes round the other pieces. Less than half of a five-letter name is two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Deliberately wrecking or obstructing a plan or machine is exactly the kind of deed that thwarts others.

clue.text: Dog's failed to start? That's an advantage

indicators.note: failing to start means the beginning never happens, so the opening letter goes

blocks.note: a basset is a short-legged hound

explanation.surface: A sluggish dog that won't get going might still be a blessing.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping the first letter of BASSET leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A useful quality or resource that benefits its owner is a plain synonym for something favourable.

clue.text: Result of getting excited before sex: blistering

indicators.note: coming before means standing in front, so the parts go in that order

blocks.note: someone worked up or het up is excited
S is the abbreviation for sex, as on forms
blistering heat is very hot

explanation.surface: A smutty Private Eye line about what follows arousal before sex.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon is surface punctuation; 'blistering' is just the last piece, not a description of the sex.
explanation.definitionFit: The final outcome or consequence of events is a standard synonym for result.

clue.text: Lord was with this ex-PM

blocks.note: surface reading: a peer accompanied by some former prime minister
setter's reading: the title Lord placed with this name forms the name of an eighteenth-century prime minister

explanation.surface: A peer once kept company with a former prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord North led the government from 1770 to 1782, losing the American colonies; the clue asks which word went with Lord.
explanation.definitionFit: Frederick North, known as Lord North, was a British prime minister, so his name identifies a former holder of that office.

clue.text: Who mocks the urethra?

blocks.note: surface reading: a person who makes fun of others
setter's reading: the tube that carries urine away from the bladder, read literally as a thing that takes it

explanation.walkthrough: To take the piss is British slang for mocking someone; the urethra literally carries urine, so it is the joke's second candidate.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who ridicules or teases people is one who takes the mickey, in vulgar British slang.

clue.text: Just imagine putting Tory leader in Ascot wear!

indicators.note: putting something in a garment places it inside
the leader of a word is the letter at its front

blocks.note: Royal Ascot is a race meeting famous for extravagant ladies' hats
opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: An amused exclamation at the thought of a Conservative leader in a racegoer's millinery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like the containment signal but works as link; the T goes between the two words of the hat phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are exclamations of surprise inviting the listener to picture something, so the phrase swaps directly.

clue.text: Up before court

blocks.note: ere is an old word for before
CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests being up before a court as a defendant; 'before' is the first piece, not an order signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Standing upright or raised vertically is what both adjectives describe, a plain synonym pair.

clue.text: It's sweeney, unfortunately, who looked on as crime was commited?

definitions.text: who looked on as crime was commited

indicators.note: an unfortunate outcome is things going wrong, so the letters fall into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
taken as written

explanation.surface: A police lament that the Flying Squad merely watched while a crime went on.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sweeney is London slang for the Flying Squad (rhyming slang, Sweeney Todd) and a 1970s TV police drama, which makes the crime surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who personally saw an offence take place and can testify about it is the meaning described.

clue.text: Hard to shake off, this independent politician, stuck in obstacle

definitions.note: the definition is a description of a thing, standing for the noun

indicators.note: something stuck in another is lodged inside it

blocks.note: I is the abbreviation for independent
a Member of Parliament
let is an old word for hindrance, as in 'without let or hindrance'

explanation.surface: An independent MP who has dug in and simply won't be removed.
explanation.walkthrough: LET as an obstacle survives in legal phrasing and in tennis, where a let is a serve obstructed by the net.
explanation.definitionFit: The shellfish clings to rocks so tightly it is famously difficult to prise away, hence its use for clingy people.

clue.text: Trump finally about to meet supreme commander on time (shopping centre)

indicators.note: the final letter alone is kept
meeting means coming up against, so the parts join end to end

blocks.note: end letter of the name
re means concerning or about
C-in-C is Commander-in-Chief
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Trump, as Commander-in-Chief, is due to arrive punctually at a mall.
explanation.walkthrough: Trump himself is a supreme commander in the surface, but only his last letter is used and the title is abbreviated separately.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a pedestrian precinct is a traffic-free area of shops, so the word denotes a shopping area.

clue.text: American in debt unceremoniously thrown in jail?

definitions.note: busted means arrested, a step short of jailed, hence the question mark

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it
done without ceremony means done roughly, without proper order

blocks.note: US is short for the United States, so American
taken as written

explanation.surface: An American who ran up debts was bundled off to prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unceremoniously thrown' sounds like the arrest itself, but 'unceremoniously' is the rearrangement signal for the debt letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for arrested by police, which typically leads to being locked up, though the question mark admits the stretch.

clue.text: Boris's opening spin on unknown cover-up

definitions.note: a cover-up is read literally: something held up as a cover

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter
in a down clue one piece placed on another sits above it

blocks.note: first letter of the name
to spin over is to roll
y is an algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: Johnson's first move is to spin his way out of a scandal being hushed up.
explanation.walkthrough: A brolly is everyday British for an umbrella. 'Cover-up' suggests a scandal, but here it is something put up to cover you.
explanation.definitionFit: An umbrella is raised overhead as protection from rain, so it is literally a cover held up.

clue.text: Humour of actress's first appearance after lap dancing

indicators.note: dancing letters jump about out of their order
making a first appearance after something means turning up behind it

blocks.note: taken as written
Cate Blanchett is the crossword's stock actress

explanation.surface: An actress's comic debut in a lap-dancing scene.
explanation.walkthrough: Humour is the verb, to indulge someone, not the noun meaning comedy; the actress's name follows the shuffled lap.
explanation.definitionFit: To humour someone is to go along with their wishes to keep them content, which is to pacify or appease them.

clue.text: "Anger" … that's how change might be presented to an American, reportedly

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by voice, so the sound counts, not the spelling

blocks.clueFragment: that's how change might be presented to an American
blocks.note: American small change comes in cents

explanation.surface: Fury at the way American shops hand back coins.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb sense is needed: to incense someone is to anger them, stressed on the second syllable, unlike the perfumed smoke.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to make someone very cross or enraged is a direct synonym of the transitive verb.

clue.text: Lord Archer-style statement, say, read backwards

indicators.note: reading backwards takes the letters from right to left

blocks.note: the novelist Jeffrey Archer was jailed for perjury, lying in court
e.g. means for example, as does say

explanation.surface: A statement in the manner of Lord Archer, whose testimony needs reading with suspicion.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeffrey Archer, a Conservative peer, served prison time in 2001 for perjury; 'Lord' opens the clue as part of his title yet is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A liege is a feudal superior to whom allegiance is owed, so it means a sovereign master.

clue.text: (& 5dn.) One's captivated by strange Ottoman quirk – speech written after it?

indicators.note: someone captivated is held captive, enclosed by their captor
strange means odd or abnormal, so the letters are in an unfamiliar order

blocks.note: a means one, as in a single thing
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone fascinated by an odd Turkish habit, with a speech set down afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' wants to be I, which leaves the letters wrong; it is A. The question mark flags a cryptic definition: in print, spoken words follow the opening inverted comma.
explanation.definitionFit: An inverted comma opens reported speech in writing, so the words spoken come after this punctuation symbol.

clue.text: State of Queen when mounting a seaman

indicators.note: in a down clue something mounting another rides on top, so it comes first

blocks.note: Q is the abbreviation for queen
taken as written
tar is an old word for a sailor

explanation.surface: A saucy Private Eye scenario about the condition of the monarch with a sailor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State of' reads as condition, but State is the definition: a Gulf country.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gulf emirate is a sovereign nation, which is one sense of a political state.

clue.text: Aim at 'snake resentment"

definitions.note: the answer takes 'to' rather than 'at', but both mean set one's sights on

blocks.note: an asp is a small venomous snake
ire is anger

explanation.surface: Targeting a reptile's bitterness.
explanation.walkthrough: The stray quotation marks are typographical; the snake and the anger simply follow one another.
explanation.definitionFit: To have an ambition and strive for something is to set one's goal on it, a close synonym.

clue.text: Money initially taken by Romney in fuel pledge

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept
something taken by another is joined to it as its companion
one thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: first letter of the word
Mitt Romney, the US Republican politician
coal is a fuel

explanation.surface: Romney pockets cash while making a promise about energy.
explanation.walkthrough: Romney's first name is needed, not the surname; together with the first M the pair sit inside the fuel.
explanation.definitionFit: A pledge is a promise binding oneself, and committal can mean committing oneself, though it more often means consigning.

clue.text: (& 26ac.) Keen PM 'ice-breaking' for a Trump sidekick

indicators.note: something breaking shatters into pieces that land in a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An eager prime minister breaking the ice with Trump's deputy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ice-breaking' reads as one word for a friendly opener, but 'ice' joins the fodder and only 'breaking' signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Trump's vice-president from 2017 to 2021 was his loyal second-in-command, fairly described as his sidekick.

clue.text: see 5dn.
Commit auto theft on reaching Spain – watch what you're doing

indicators.note: reaching something means arriving next to it, so the parts join in sequence

blocks.note: stealing a car is taking it
E is the international vehicle code for Spain (España)

explanation.surface: A car thief arriving in Spain is warned to be careful.
explanation.walkthrough: The car registration code for Spain comes from its own name, España.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are warnings to be careful and attentive, so the phrase is an idiomatic equivalent of the command.

clue.text: Credit given to fundamentalists for disaster

indicators.note: something given to another is added on beside it

blocks.note: CR is the accounting abbreviation for credit
the Islamist militant group

explanation.surface: Financing extremists would be catastrophic.
explanation.walkthrough: CR appears in bank statements against money paid in.
explanation.definitionFit: A time of acute danger or calamity is close in sense to a catastrophe, though weaker.
